cases.title: Tbilisi–Rustavi road, Ponichala: homes bought out, red-list trees felled
cases.place: Ponichala, Tbilisi, and the Tbilisi–Rustavi highway section, Georgia
cases.point: Ponichala, on the Tbilisi–Rustavi highway alignment, where the complainant buildings 12 v/g, 16 a/b and 28a stand (approximate; the ADB reports do not give coordinates)

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loan 3063 for Tranche 3 of the Sustainable Urban Transport Investment Program. ADB provided $73 million of a $118.2 million total project cost. The project was classed A for involuntary resettlement and B for environment, but was monitored as if it were category A for environment. Revised closing date 18 July 2020 (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Second Annual Monitoring Report, 11 November 2019).

cases.conditions: The loan financed a section of the Tbilisi–Rustavi road. At the borrower's request the road scope was cut from 6.8 km to 3.5 km. Land acquisition and resettlement plans (LARP 2a and 2b) governed the buy-outs, and ADB's Compliance Review Panel imposed a remedial action plan after finding the project non-compliant in six areas, including noise, vibration and vulnerable groups; the remedial measures were disclosed in April and May 2018 (ADB semi-annual social monitoring report, January–June 2018; ADB CRP, Second Annual Monitoring Report, 2019).
cases.community: ADB's own monitoring records what was taken. Under LARP 2a, 243 of 244 properties were acquired; the only one left was the GMP Pharmaceutical Company. Under LARP 2b, all 192 properties were acquired, which the report breaks down as all 151 privately owned properties and all 41 apartments. A two-storey building with 41 apartments was recommended for dismantling after a 2015 structural study, and the Municipal Development Fund demolished a state-owned two-storey building after a request on 11 January 2018 and disposed of the debris. Compensation was paid into bank accounts; the report gives no amounts and no relocation counts (ADB semi-annual social monitoring report, January–June 2018). For the project as a whole the Compliance Review Panel records 312 land plots, 29.5 hectares and 692 structures to be demolished (82 residential, 90 industrial and commercial, 520 minor), affecting 282 households and 33 businesses. The same report records that 57 trees on Georgia's national red list were cut from the National Forest Park and that replanting had not happened by November 2019, and that a construction dump of about 160,000 cubic metres sat next to Ponichala's residential and industrial areas. A 60-metre retaining wall foundation sits in the Mtkvari riverbed, three 20-metre sections of it built in July and August 2019 (ADB CRP, Second Annual Monitoring Report, 11 November 2019). Residents of three Ponichala apartment blocks complained to ADB about noise and vibration: 81 residents of building 12 v/g on 14 March 2016, 72 residents of building 16 a/b on 10 November 2016, and 30 residents of building 28a on 21 June 2018. The Panel's finding for building 28a was 'likely harm'; its 2019 report does not record any confirmed physical damage to the complainants' buildings, and says no construction took place in their areas during the monitoring period. Residents of Marneuli Street complained in early 2018 about vibration from machinery, and the fund and contractor identified a method to stop that exposure. A fourth complaint, from 18 residents of Marneuli Street on 11 October 2018, concerned resettlement compensation and was found ineligible at that time because the parties were still trying to settle it. Of 95 visually impaired residents identified in the resettlement plan, 10 had died, 8 had moved out, 35 attended a meeting with relatives and 42 were contacted individually (ADB CRP, 2019).
cases.outcome: ADB's Compliance Review Panel found the project non-compliant in six areas and monitored a remedial action plan. By November 2019 the noise abatement package for the Ponichala stretch — a 560-metre acoustic tunnel, 880 metres of 5-metre wall and 188 metres of 8-metre wall — had not been started, and the measures to remove loose parts from buildings and secure annexes were listed as not yet implemented. The complainants' properties were not needed by the project, so they were not covered by the land acquisition and resettlement plan (ADB CRP, 2019).

cases.title: Peshawar landfill at Ghari Faiz Ullah: 99 acres taken, open dumping and unpaid owners
cases.place: Ghari Faiz Ullah, about 19 km south of the Peshawar Ring Road, Peshawar district, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
cases.point: Approximate. The ADB corrective action plan places the landfill at Ghari Faiz Ullah, about 19 km south of the Peshawar Ring Road, and gives no coordinates; the point is set in that direction from the city and is not a surveyed location.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loan 4160-PAK, US$380 million from ordinary capital resources, and Grant 0816-PAK, US$5 million from the Asian Development Fund, both approved 10 December 2021, signed 15 December 2021, effective 11 April 2022, closing 30 June 2028. Project 51036-002, classed A for environment and A for involuntary resettlement (ADB project page).

lenders.name: Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank
lenders.role: Loan 8412-PAK, US$200 million of co-financing, approved 16 December 2021, signed 15 December 2021, effective 11 May 2022 (ADB project page).

cases.conditions: The money funds water, sewerage, solid waste and green infrastructure in five Khyber Pakhtunkhwa cities — Abbottabad, Kohat, Mardan, Mingora and Peshawar — with 24 subprojects approved; ADB says up to 3.5 million people will benefit (ADB project page). For the Peshawar landfill subproject ADB required an Implementable Corrective Action Plan with a budget of PKR 238.75 million, about US$1.5 million, and made civil works conditional on the plan being carried out in full (ADB, Implementable Corrective Action Plan, April 2023).
cases.community: ADB's own corrective action plan for the Peshawar Integrated Solid Waste Management System records that 99 acres, or 792 kanal, were acquired in 2017 under the urgency clause of the Land Acquisition Act 1894, and that 234 landowners are affected. The document says the acquisition 'did not meet the principles of ADB's Safeguard Policy Statement (SPS) 2009', naming the urgency clause, which 'denies the people right to appeal', and valuation below replacement cost. One displaced person 'lost all his productive land i.e. 100% (6.25 acres)'; another lost more than 10% of his land. Two mud-and-brick structures used as farm-labour housing, one tube well, 90 acacia trees and 30 orange trees are affected, and the structures were still standing and in use when the survey was done. 63 displaced persons are classed vulnerable; of 43 vulnerable landowners, 39 are below the poverty line and 4 are women-headed households. 20 informal waste collectors depend on recyclables from the dumpsite. Since the government took possession the site has been used for open waste dumping. Consultation participants said that 'the entire area is engulfed with very bad odor', that 'The incidence of diseases in both men and women and especially children has increased', that water-borne disease was rising, that 'The open dumping has affected the drinking water quality', and that heavy trucks had damaged roads. The Board of Revenue assessed compensation of PKR 159 million and payments began in May 2020; by the date of the plan 149 of the 234 landowners, about 64 per cent, had been paid and 85 had not — 'Payments to 85 landowners of PKR 39 million is pending' — with the delays put down to mutation problems, minors, missing bank accounts and absentee owners. An independent valuation found land had been valued 31.43 per cent below replacement cost, a gap of PKR 49.6 million: PKR 157.8 million as set by the Land Acquisition Collector against PKR 207.4 million under the valuation. Displaced persons said the government offered '30% less value for the land'. Nine consultation sessions were held between March 2020 and May 2021 with 48 participants, 14 of them women (ADB, Implementable Corrective Action Plan, April 2023).
cases.outcome: The corrective action plan was to be finished by the end of March 2023 and verified by an external monitor in April 2023, with civil works held back until it was complete (ADB, Implementable Corrective Action Plan, April 2023). A separate compliance review request on the wider project, CRP 2022/5, was received on 27 December 2022 and withdrawn the next day; ADB's accountability mechanism page says the complainants withdrew after receiving what they considered adequate compensation, and the Compliance Review Panel made no findings (ADB Accountability Mechanism). ADB's register holds 64 entries under this project name, the most recent SPF-2026-44-15-0264.

cases.confidence_note: The land taking, the under-valuation, the unpaid owners and the open dumping all come from ADB's own April 2023 corrective action plan, a document ADB published under the project. Timing needs stating plainly: the 99 acres were acquired in 2017, four years before ADB's loan was approved on 10 December 2021. What happened under ADB and AIIB financing is the continuation — 85 of 234 owners still unpaid, the site still being open-dumped, and ADB's own finding that the 2017 acquisition fell short of its 2009 Safeguard Policy Statement. The reports of odour, rising illness and spoiled drinking water are what consultation participants told the project's own consultants; no health study was opened. The document's figures are internally inconsistent in places — it says all the scavengers are teenage boys aged 13 to 18 while its Annex 3 lists ages from 5 to 53, and some land and vulnerability totals are garbled. I read about 50 of its 64 pages; the text was cut off part way through Annex 6.

cases.title: Sahiwal water and sanitation works: 196 acres notified for the plant, sewage standing at homes
cases.point: Sahiwal city, where the ADB-financed wastewater treatment plant site and the PICIIP-03 Lot 2 sewer works are. Neither ADB document opened gives coordinates.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: US$200 million of a US$250 million Punjab Intermediate Cities Improvement Investment Project, project 46526-007, approved 19 September 2017 with the closing date extended to 30 June 2026; the remaining US$50 million came from the Government of Pakistan (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/6; ADB problem-solving story).

cases.conditions: The loan funded water and sanitation works in Sahiwal and Sialkot. Contract PICIIP-03 Package Sahiwal Water and Sanitation Lot 2 was awarded on 13 October 2020 and handed to the Sahiwal Water and Sanitation Agency on 30 June 2026. ADB screened Lot 2 as category C for involuntary resettlement on the basis that the sewer works stayed inside the existing government right-of-way and needed no land acquisition or displacement. A corrective action plan was signed on 27 April 2026 (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/6).
cases.community: Two things happened in Sahiwal. For the wastewater treatment plant, the government moved to acquire 196.35 acres. In October 2022 eighteen households who owned 40 of those acres complained to ADB's Office of the Special Project Facilitator that the compensation was below the replacement cost of similar nearby land and that consultation had been inadequate; two more households complained in May 2023 and the cases were joined. Farmers described the land as their only source of livelihood. ADB and the project unit redesigned the plant so about 20 acres on the northern side could go back; the Punjab Board of Revenue then ruled that land could not be denotified for some owners only, so the whole original group had to buy the land back, and the area denotified was cut from 20.22 acres to 15.275 acres. A memorandum of understanding was signed in Lahore on 20 January 2024 and the complainants agreed to drop their court case. By May 2024, 17 of the 18 households had been paid; the last was waiting on a land transfer to legal heirs (ADB problem-solving story, as reported by Devdiscourse). Separately, on the Lot 2 sewer works, two residents of Sahiwal complained to ADB on 15 June 2026 that an approximately 1,800-foot sewer pipeline had been laid in a zigzag alignment close to their homes, that sewage stood in front of houses for about three months with foul odours, that trenches were left open and access blocked, that rain waterlogged the area, and that household sewer connections were lost for more than two months, with substandard temporary connections put in during June 2026. One wrote that the sewage was 'damaging to our house' and that the family's shops lost money. The Compliance Review Panel records that the authorities 'accepted that overflowing and stagnant sewage water was occurring' during the bypass period, and that the complainants and their families 'faced grave inconvenience, particularly due to the foul odor and restricted access'. The Panel found these construction impacts real and recognised by the project, and found them addressed by the time of its field visit. Sand filling and household connections were finished by 22 June 2026 and the final asphalt on 20 August 2026 (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/6).
cases.suppression: The complainants also reported intimidation, threats of criminal proceedings, a shove on 15 June 2026, and that one family was confined overnight on 19 April 2026. ADB Management said it found no evidence that project personnel made the threats. The Compliance Review Panel said it could not determine whether the incidents occurred and urged Management to stay alert to retaliation risks (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/6).
cases.outcome: The 2022 land complaint ended in the January 2024 memorandum, the part-denotification of 15.275 acres and payment to 17 of 18 households by May 2024 (ADB problem-solving story, as reported by Devdiscourse). The 2026 sewer complaint was found ineligible for compliance review: the Compliance Review Panel judged the concerns localised rather than systemic, found the harms adequately addressed with no ongoing harm, and so found the request outside paragraphs 179 and 180 of the Accountability Mechanism Policy. Ten of the project's 12 subprojects were finished by the loan closing date; the Sialkot wastewater plant and water metering were left to the government to fund. ADB's register holds 20 entries under this project name, the most recent SPF-2026-27-07-0247.

cases.confidence_note: The sewage standing in front of homes is not only the complainants' word for it: the Compliance Review Panel records that the authorities accepted it was happening, and the Panel found the construction impacts real. The Panel also found them already fixed, and it made no finding on the shop losses, which rest on the complaint alone. The land acquisition account comes from a Devdiscourse summary of ADB's own problem-solving story, not from the ADB report itself, which I did not open; the acreage denotified and the 17-of-18 payment figures carry that limit. The Panel found no private land was acquired for the Lot 2 sewer, which is a separate matter from the plant site. The intimidation and overnight confinement are unresolved: ADB Management says there is no evidence project staff made threats, and the Panel could not determine whether the incidents happened. I read the Panel report's body and complaint annex; the text was cut off part way through Management's response at paragraph 25, so I did not see the rest of Management's answer on consultation or retaliation.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loan 3520-GEO to the Government of Georgia, agreement signed 12 June 2017 (ADB compliance monitoring report filed under project 50064). ADB's share of the financing is EUR 108.2 million (AIIB project document).

lenders.name: Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank
lenders.role: US$114.0 million; the AIIB report gives an approval date of 15 June 2017 without saying whether that date applies to the loan, and its loan agreement was signed 17 June 2017 (AIIB project document; ADB compliance monitoring report).

cases.conditions: The loans fund a new two-lane bypass of about 14.3 km on the East–West Highway, skirting the port city of Batumi, at a total project cost of US$315.2 million (AIIB project document). Land was bought out under a land acquisition and resettlement plan administered by the Roads Department (ADB, Office of the Special Project Facilitator, Lessons Learned, 2020).
cases.community: ADB's published account of the project's land take records 963 privately owned land parcels affected, 46 hectares of private land to be acquired, and 741 affected households containing 4,051 people. Of those, the document says 369 households 'have been or will be' physically displaced, and 562 households, 3,024 people, are severely affected, meaning displaced or losing 10 per cent or more of their income-producing assets. On 2 October 2018 a household whose land and assets had been acquired complained to ADB's Office of the Special Project Facilitator that the Roads Department had paid about GEL 100,000, roughly $40,000, below market value. The household had objected repeatedly and hired its own valuer, whose figure was much higher, and the ADB account says that 'Despite these objections and complaints with the local GRM, the complainant's position had been dismissed every time.' It had signed the contract reluctantly after a government letter said expropriation would follow a refusal: 'The complainant was worried that it would lose everything and thus, reluctantly agreed to the compensation offered.' ADB hired Colliers International, which inspected the property on 5 March 2019 and valued it at the project's own valuation date of 1 November 2016; the independent valuation 'determined that the value of the property was about 20% higher than the original project valuation'. The same document lists the other complaints the project drew: compensation rates, inclusion in the resettlement plan, property registration, damage to infrastructure or assets, a plant appraisal, and one about drinking water and a new fence (ADB, Office of the Special Project Facilitator, Lessons Learned, 2020).
cases.outcome: After ADB-facilitated talks with the government in May 2019 the Roads Department reopened the case and negotiated a settlement on the gap between what it had paid and the independent valuation. The new contract was signed on 27 June 2019 and full payment confirmed on 29 June 2019. ADB's office recorded that the grievance mechanism was too slow and not neutral enough to catch the problem early, that complainants felt consultation was neither meaningful nor timely, and that the root cause was poorly substantiated valuations. The document does not state the final settlement amount. ADB's register holds five complaints under this project name, from SPF-2017-09-01-0066 to SPF-2026-42-01-0262.

cases.title: Greater Colombo sewerage works: a damaged house and six years of claims
cases.place: Colombo Municipal Council area, Sri Lanka
cases.point: Approximate, in the Colombo Municipal Council area. ADB's reports do not name the street or ward where the complainant's house stands.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loan 2557-SRI, US$80.00 million from ordinary capital resources, and Loan 2558-SRI, US$20.00 million from the Asian Development Fund, both approved 28 September 2009, signed 18 December 2009, effective 9 April 2010. Project 36173-013, classed B for environment and B for involuntary resettlement. Loan 2558 closed 17 April 2023 and Loan 2557 on 7 December 2023. The ADB project page lists no co-financing (ADB project page).

cases.conditions: The loans paid for upgrading Colombo's sewerage — pumping stations, sewer pipes and discharge outfalls — plus institutional strengthening and project management, with the Colombo Municipal Council as executing agency and the National Water Supply and Drainage Board implementing one component under a separate project agreement (ADB project page).
cases.community: A household in the Colombo Municipal Council area complained three times to ADB's Office of the Special Project Facilitator about the sewerage construction, 'alleging impact on property and health issues due to the Project construction'. The Colombo Municipal Council paid the complainant SLRs121,000 on 5 December 2017, which ADB's report describes as 'the estimated cost of repair works directly related to his house'. The complainant's mother was hospitalised; the council rejected the claim that the construction caused it, but by November 2018 the complainant said the contractor's insurer had paid 75 per cent of the medical costs, and after a Grievance Redress Committee meeting on 26 November 2018 the council paid the remaining 25 per cent, SLRs41,852.33. The committee also recommended the council pay for the mother's alternative accommodation while repairs were done, and the council agreed to pay SLRs5,250 over a discrepancy in an earlier hospitalisation. A further SLRs50,000 was held available for repairs, but only if a council inspector was on site and confirmed a cost overrun, and SLRs57,500 claimed for the cost of the repair estimate was still under review by higher council authorities. The complainants put daily hospital costs at about SLRs26,000; the hospital told the council about SLRs9,000 (ADB, Office of the Special Project Facilitator, Final Report, October 2023).
cases.outcome: The first complaint, SPF-2017-04-01-0061 of 19 April 2017, was found not eligible on 18 May 2017 because the household had not first tried ADB's operations department. A second, SPF-2018-10-02-0079 of 11 September 2018, about how the hospitalisation claim was assessed, was found not eligible on 9 October 2018 because the council would not engage further; ADB's page records 'OSPF intervention was not useful.' The third, SPF-2019-12-03-0092 of 22 November 2019, was found eligible on 15 January 2020. ADB's office found that almost all the household's payment requests about property and well-being had already been paid or approved by the council, and advised the household that the council's final offer 'appeared to be consistent with ADB policies'. The household did not accept it, the council then declined further problem-solving, and the office closed the case in its final report of October 2023. An earlier request, 2017-4 of 29 March 2017, was forwarded to the facilitator on 19 April 2017 (ADB Accountability Mechanism; ADB, Final Report, October 2023).

What is documented is that the Colombo Municipal Council paid SLRs121,000 as the estimated cost of repairs 'directly related to his house', which records damage the implementing agency accepted and paid for. cases.community: ADB's own verification identified 275 affected persons along the two work corridors: 121 under the SD13 sewerage and drainage package and 154 under WS16. ADB Management says the impacts 'principally comprised temporary disruption and income loss to roadside vendors during pipe-laying works', that the project had assumed a 10-day disruption and then paid 'uniform livelihood assistance equivalent to 30 days of income loss to all affected persons', and that everyone identified was paid, in some cases above the approved entitlement, by bank transfer and cheque. For SD13 the resettlement plan had estimated 24 affected persons against the 121 later verified; Management says the increase 'does not indicate any concealment or underreporting'. The project's three-tier grievance mechanism recorded 1,647 cases across the programme, 81 under SD13 and 29 under WS16, and Management says 'The records do not show any unresolved grievances'. Six vendors from Kolkata, represented by Growthwatch India and asking for confidentiality, complained to ADB's Compliance Review Panel on 13 June 2026, attaching a list of about 124 other affected people. They said they had traded from the same spots on government land for about 25 to 30 years, that their shops were dismantled in 2019 at their own cost, and that 'we were prohibited from returning to our sites of operation and some of us even detained'. They said they had been 'reduced to vending from hand-held tea or other carts' or to daily wage work, that some had moved away from the area, and that they received INR 15,000 in August 2019, which they considered inadequate: 'We are still waiting to have our previous shops back, and with them, our former earnings.' ADB Management says the opposite on the central point — 'ADB staff found no records showing that the Project required the permanent demolition of roadside shops' — and that neither the resettlement plan nor the verification found physical displacement from housing. In August 2019 the NGO INSAF raised the case of four roadside shopkeepers; ADB's review then found their structures intact and that they had been paid. Management attributes what happened after 2023 to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation's own road-widening, which began on 17 February 2023 and which it says ADB neither financed nor supervised (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/4).
cases.suppression: The complainants say some of them were detained when they tried to re-establish their businesses, and that they faced intimidation when they raised complaints. ADB Management ties the alleged intimidation to the period after 2023 and to the municipal road-widening rather than to the ADB-financed works. The Compliance Review Panel made no finding either way (ADB Compliance Review Panel, Report on Eligibility, Request 2026/4).
cases.outcome: The Compliance Review Panel found the complaint ineligible on 2 September 2026 under paragraph 142(iv) of the 2012 Accountability Mechanism Policy, which bars complaints filed two or more years after the loan closing date. It found the formal closing date was 31 August 2023, so the window shut on 31 August 2025, nine months before the complaint was filed on 13 June 2026. The 14 June 2024 date on ADB's Project Data Sheet was the financial closing date, not the loan closing date; the Panel found the data sheet's presentation unclear and ADB's March 2026 email to the complainants unclear too, but said this had not cost them the deadline because the period had already expired when they asked. It said it had no discretion to substitute the financial closing date. The Panel made no finding on ADB's compliance, on the alleged harms, or on causation, and did not reach the tests of noncompliance, direct and material harm or seriousness.

What is in dispute is how bad it was. The complainants say their shops were dismantled in 2019, that they were kept from returning, that some were detained, and that INR 15,000 did not cover the loss. No independent source on the vendors' side was opened. cases.title: Malolos–Clark Railway: tagged in 2018, still waiting, and a 2026 complaint of demolition without compensation
cases.place: San Fernando and Angeles, Pampanga, along the Malolos–Clark railway right-of-way, Philippines
cases.point: Approximate, at Barangay Maimpis, San Fernando City, Pampanga, one of the places along the right-of-way named in VERA Files' reporting.

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: US$2.75 billion for civil works — viaducts, stations, tunnels and depot buildings. The first tranche of US$1.3 billion, P66.83 billion at the 11 July 2019 exchange rate, was signed on 11 July 2019; its validity was extended from 21 December 2021 to 21 December 2022 and then to 30 June 2024. ADB had disbursed P47.40 billion by December 2023 (VERA Files). ADB project 52083-001 (ADB Accountability Mechanism).

lenders.name: Japan International Cooperation Agency
lenders.role: US$2 billion for tracks, electrification, signalling, telecommunications, rolling stock and consulting services (VERA Files).

cases.conditions: The loans fund the 53 km Malolos–Clark section of the North–South Commuter Railway. JICA recommended a consistent 30-metre right-of-way where the legacy Philippine National Railways corridor is about 10 to 20 metres wide, so more land had to be bought, most of it in dense residential areas. The Philippine government paid P74.67 million in commitment fees on undrawn loans in 2022 alone, at 0.15 per cent a year on undrawn amounts, which VERA Files attributes to the delays. An ADB cost–benefit analysis put the economic internal rate of return at 12.3 per cent and said the project 'remains viable in all cases' in the scenarios it tested, including a two-year delay (VERA Files).
cases.community: Rosa Lebosana, 41, of Barangay Maimpis in San Fernando City, has lived since 2003 in a 50-square-metre house with her husband and three children. Her house was surveyed and tagged on 9 November 2018 and sits partly inside the 30-metre right-of-way. Six years after the tagging she said the Department of Transportation had not followed through and local leaders could not answer her questions; her family had still not moved. Her relocation option is Barangay Panipuan, about 9.7 km away, where relocated families take a housing loan from the National Housing Authority and get a land title from the local government. JICA's 2018 census recorded 1,416 potentially affected households; National Housing Authority data for 2024 showed the number of affected informal settler families had risen by about 108.70 per cent. As of September 2024 fewer than 5 per cent of affected informal settler families had been verified and resettled, and in Pampanga 112 of 1,936 had been relocated. By October 2024 the Department of Transportation had acquired 31 parcels, 4.9 hectares, of the estimated 45.5 hectares needed. In San Fernando, 67 row houses in Barangay Calulut had been built and occupied and 312 units in Barangay Panipuan were ready for occupancy by October 2024, while a planned 280-unit site in Panipuan had not started because the land has to be reclassified out of a Strategic Agriculture and Fisheries Development Zone. Demolition of houses along the main line cannot go ahead until replacement housing is ready: without those prerequisites, VERA Files reports, 'the demolition of houses along the main railway line cannot proceed.' On 7 October 2026 a complaint was filed with ADB's accountability mechanism against the project, SPF-2026-43-04-0263, with the issue recorded as 'House demolition without compensation' (ADB Accountability Mechanism).
cases.outcome: Construction in San Fernando was 28.97 per cent complete as of August 2024, and the 53 km section's completion moved from 2024 to 2028; San Fernando's own projected completion moved from 2027 to 2028 and then to 2029. VERA Files traces the delay to the 2018–19 parcellary plans, which contained errors found when work resumed in 2022 and had to be revalidated; the National Economic and Development Authority's August 2024 portfolio review blamed 'prolonged review and approval' of parcellary plans that 'did not meet set standards'. Contract Package No. 03, covering Angeles and San Fernando, was worst hit; in Angeles only about 30 per cent of the area for package N-03 was workable. The transport department's right-of-way team had four members at the start and 48 by October 2024, against a target of 137. Its planning undersecretary called the lack of on-ground staff the real root cause and said 'Just imagine the burden if you are one person handling 200 parcels.' Angeles City's planning office said the department had not given it parcellary maps showing affected areas and structures, which made issuing building permits near the railway harder. ADB's register holds five complaints under the Malolos–Clark and South Commuter railway project names between 2025 and 2026.

cases.confidence_note: The documented loss here is land taken and households moved: 31 parcels and 4.9 hectares acquired by October 2024, 112 of 1,936 informal settler families relocated in Pampanga by September 2024, and 67 row houses built and occupied at Barangay Calulut, all reported by VERA Files from Department of Transportation and National Housing Authority data. Relocated families take on a housing loan from the National Housing Authority and move about 9.7 km. The other documented harm is the wait: one named household tagged on 9 November 2018 and still in place six years later, with fewer than 5 per cent of affected families verified and resettled as of September 2024. The October 2026 ADB complaint alleging house demolition without compensation is an allegation on an ADB register page with no outcome recorded; nothing is concluded from it here. VERA Files reports no completed demolitions and gives no compensation amounts. The ADB and JICA loan figures come from VERA Files, not from the loan documents, which I did not open. The lead that produced this case also named Cambodia–Laos Greater Mekong tourism infrastructure and the Philippine South Commuter Railway; nothing was documented for either and they are not covered here.

dropped.reason: Fails tests 2 and 3: no construction, so no harm. A 2024 NGO report filed to the Council of Europe (rm.coe.int, the Svaneti/Nenskra complainants' report, which I read in full at about 1,400 words) records that local people say work has not started on Nenskra and that no construction company had been selected, with the government saying it expected works to resume 'by the end of the year, 2024 at the latest'. OC Media (2020) records that construction has been on hold since Salini Impregilo left in October 2018, and that Bankwatch's field investigation found over 200 people 'would lose' homes, land or pastures — future loss. Bankwatch's own September 2017 blog says pasture and wooden cabins 'would be temporarily or permanently lost' and records no confirmed loss. The EBRD and EIB complaint mechanisms found the project non-compliant with their standards on land acquisition, resettlement, economic displacement, Indigenous issues, cultural heritage, disclosure and engagement, but those are findings about the banks, not records of harm, and neither bank had signed its loan agreement (EBRD $214 million, EIB $150 million, both approved). ADB is listed only as a prospective investor. One item I could not open: business-humanrights.org's summary of a later NGO report saying JSC Nenskra Hydro failed to provide adequate compensation for people affected — both the English and French URLs returned a client error from the site and nothing of either page was retrieved, so whether land was in fact acquired is unresolved and someone should retry that page.

dropped.candidate: Assam Solar Project, Karbi Anglong, CRP 2024/8 and 2025/3
dropped.reason: Fails tests 2 and 3. PUCL's account of the Karbi people's struggle (pucl.org, read in full) describes the 18,000 bighas in East Karbi Anglong as land that 'would be taken up', the 24 villages and more than 20,000 people as those who 'would be directly affected', and residents' fear of losing their homes; it reports no crop losses, no fencing, no evictions and no arrests, and names no fact-finding team's findings on the ground. ADB withdrew the $434.25 million loan request in May 2025 before approval, so no ADB money was in place when anything could have happened; PUCL's own postscript records the withdrawal and says the struggle to cancel the project continues. PUCL also gives the loan as both $435.25 million and $434.25 million and does not explain the gap. A separate report that India's National Commission for Scheduled Tribes has sought a report on the 18,000 bighas after the cancellation was seen only as a headline and not opened.

dropped.candidate: Georgian Railway Green Bond (Zestaponi–Kharagauli–Khashuri landslides), CRP 2025/9
dropped.reason: Fails the link test, on the office's own words. The harm is real and documented: Democracy and Freedom Watch reports a roughly three-kilometre rupture across the mountainside at Khemaghali and Ghverki in Kharagauli municipality, first noticed as cracks on 26 May 2025, with about 107 households in the two villages before the slide, most told to leave and rent elsewhere, most homes in Khemaghali abandoned with cracked walls, government rent support of up to 500 lari a month and many villagers left off the registries. But the Compliance Review Panel found the complaint outside the scope of compliance review because the alleged harms were not related to ADB-financed components, stating that 'The construction of the tunnels falls strictly outside the activities financed by ADB' — ADB's $20 million in Georgian Railway green bonds since 2021 went to substation renovation, bridges, culverts, track laying, electrification and water works, not tunnelling (Sakartvelos Ambebi, reporting the Panel's decision). Residents say experts privately linked the slide to blasting for railway construction in 2019–2022; no official geological finding on the cause has been published. If a future document ties the blasting to an ADB-financed component, this becomes a case.

dropped.candidate: Delhi–Meerut Regional Rapid Transit (ADB and AIIB; SPF-2022-14-02-0134)
dropped.reason: Fails test 2 on what I could open: the harm is feared, not recorded. ADB's complaint page for SPF-2022-14-02-0134 (filed 11 October 2022, found eligible 5 December 2022, review and assessment report issued 13 January 2025) lists only issue categories — resettlement, compensation and valuation; noise and vibration; easement rights, environment and safety. Devdiscourse's account of ADB's own problem-solving story records that residents of a New Delhi colony feared 'noise pollution, constant vibrations from passing trains', visual intrusion, falling property values and risks to children and the elderly, and it does not report that cracks or structural damage had occurred. Twenty-four apartments in three blocks were first notified for acquisition and, after the alignment was revised, eight 'were to be acquired'; the other sixteen households were excluded. Specialists hired by ADB's office found the chosen alignment 'the least harmful and within the policy framework' against ADB's 2009 Safeguard Policy Statement, Indian courts upheld the decision and an appeal was dismissed, and a February 2024 memorandum with eight of the sixteen households provided temporary relocation support, a baseline structural stability survey funded by ADB's office and a commitment to repair verified damage, with pre-construction surveys done for 14 of the 16 apartments by June 2024. Measures to catch damage if it happens are not damage. The ADB publication 'A Rail Too Far?' (June 2025, 16 pages) would be the place to check: its landing page served only metadata, abstract and contents, and the PDF itself was not opened. If its text records damage found by those surveys, this becomes a case.
